newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU mulls lira management if Italy outside EMU.
newsitem.headline: EU mulls lira management if Italy outside EMU.

text.p: Italy's exclusion from the first wave of countries joining a single European currency should enhance the euro's initial credibility, but how the lira is managed thereafter may be more important, analysts say.

There is a growing recognition among economists, fueled largely by the European Commission's stern warning to Rome that it must do more to bring public expenditure under control, that Italy will not be a founding member of the single currency.

In sharply worded language, delivered at a meeting of EU finance ministers on Monday, Rome was told that further measures were needed to put it on a path of sustainable budgetary convergence with other EU countries.
Underneath the technical jargon was a clear signal -- first wave membership in the euro was looking dim.
Conversely, the message to Spain and Portugal was upbeat and congratulatory, praising both countries on their recent efforts to slash spending.
With the two Club-Med countries looking much better placed for early EMU entry, analysts believe the markets' perceived credibility of economic and monetary union (EMU) is unlikely to suffer.
"I'm not sure the inclusion of Spain and Portugal would have a marked impact on the credibility of EMU," says Martin Brookes, economist at Goldman Sachs in London.

The reasons behind the benign outlook are several, not least the relatively small share of trade the two countries have with most core European countries. Italy, on the other hand, has an enormous flow of trade with countries like Germany and France.
The heavy volume of goods and services between these countries has in the past prompted complaints about the competitive threat a weak lira poses to industries in Europe's larger economies.
The French have been most vocal in this area.

So while Italy's initial exclusion from EMU might be viewed favourably by markets, the German public, and central bankers at the future European Central Bank (ECB), the stability of the lira against the euro is what some believe could ultimately matter most to the single currency's credibility.

"If Italy is not in the first wave of EMU but gets some guarantee that the exchange rate of the lira will be defended by the ECB, in that case the euro will have high credibility," says Eric Chaney, economist at Morgan Stanley in Paris.
Under a revamped Exchange Rate Mechanism, dubbed ERM2, currencies outside the EMU area will be linked to the euro in relatively wide trading bands.

The agreement allows the ECB to intervene in support of a currency outside the zone, but importantly, there is the option for the bank to suspend intervention if it believes that price stability among EMU members is threatened.

Analysts say it is in the best interests for those inside EMU not to let a situation develop where the lira comes under speculative attack -- prompted either by political turmoil or more fundamental worries over its budgetary and economic performance.
But just how such a goal is balanced with the overriding mandate of price stability, one that is enshrined in the Maastricht Treaty, is a question to which few have an answer.

At best, some expect any future government in Italy to be cognizant of the risks it would face by running excessive deficits and, perhaps more importantly, by failing to engage in much needed pension reform.
"There is a risk that the lira could come under speculative attack, but it's up to the government to pursue a clear consolidation course," says Werner Becker, economist at Deutsche Bank in Frankfurt.
But in the debate over how political influence might be brought to bear on a future ECB, the Italian question may be the first and most important test of its credibility and that of EMU.
